answer.rationale: Memory c2 confirms the low-cost vendor was successfully onboarded before with accurate invoicing, supporting a switch. Memory c1 confirms that renewal with the incumbent avoids migration work and interruption—this is the main risk to weigh against the 18% mandate. The current quote from the low-cost vendor meets the finance mandate alone, and memory c2 shows the vendor can deliver reliably. However, memory c1's lesson about stability is important: the assembly line is at 94% with no buffer, so any onboarding hiccup is costly. Given that the low-cost vendor was already onboarded before (memory c2), the migration risk is lower than a first-time switch. The 14-day deadline and lack of auto-renewal make inaction equivalent to losing the primary supply contract. The primary objective is to minimize total cost without increasing delivery risk; the low-cost vendor's prior performance record (memory c2) and the fact that their quote alone meets the 18% cut make switching the strongest single action. Memory c6 (multi-year commitments unlocking volume pricing) is noted but would require negotiation time we don't have in 14 days and doesn't address the immediate mandate as directly. Memory c4 (renegotiation) is also relevant but secondary to the switch decision given the tight timeline. Memory c5 (deferral) is not viable because the contract does not auto-renew and deferral would create a supply gap with no buffer. Memory c3 (second source) is valuable but we can only make one decision this cycle, and adding a second source doesn't address the primary contract expiration.
